title: Major incidents
blurb: Define major, critical and business continuity incidents, give an M/ETHANE report, triage with the NHS MITT and know your role in the response.
question: At a coach crash, a nurse finds a man who cannot walk, is breathing, answers when spoken to, and has a respiratory rate of 18 and a heart rate of 112. Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool, what priority is he?

teach.body: The Cabinet Office and JESIP define a major incident as an event or situation with a range of serious consequences that requires special arrangements to be implemented by one or more emergency responder agencies. In the NHS this includes numbers or types of casualties that normal arrangements cannot handle. In plain English: so many people need help, or the situation is so serious, that services must switch to their emergency plans. Nurses at every level have a defined role (proficiency P6.12).

teach.h: Roles at different levels of seniority
teach.body: NHS organisations run incidents through strategic, tactical and operational command. Staff follow their role-specific action cards. A ward nurse in charge may be asked to create capacity, for example identifying patients who can safely be discharged or moved, and to release staff when the incident team requests them. Off-duty staff are called in through the trust's process so that the right skills arrive when needed. Shared situational awareness and clear communication are JESIP principles.
teach.cite: NHS England EPRR Framework; JESIP principles for joint working

teach.h: If you are first at a scene, off duty
items: Check the scene is safe for you before approaching (Code 15.3: take account of your own safety).
Call 999 and give a clear M/ETHANE-style report.
Control catastrophic bleeding and open airways: the first steps of triage.
Help within the limits of your knowledge and competence (Code 15.1–15.2) and hand over to the emergency services.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Rhys at a coach crash
teach.body: Rhys reaches a casualty who cannot walk but is breathing and answers his name. He is an adult, breathing rate 18 (within 12–23), heart rate 112. Following MITT in order: no catastrophic bleeding, not walking, breathing, responds to voice, over 2, rate 12–23, heart rate 100 or more, so he is P1. A second casualty with identical findings but a heart rate of 88 would be P2.

teach.text: Walking casualties are P3, but they may be compensating for serious injuries: reassess them early. And any non-walking child judged under 2 years old is P1, whatever the other findings.

items: Major incident: serious consequences needing special arrangements by one or more responder agencies.
EPRR levels: business continuity, critical, major.
M/ETHANE: Major incident, Exact location, Type, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services.
MITT order: catastrophic bleeding, walking, breathing, voice, age over 2, breathing rate 12–23, heart rate 100 or more.
Follow your action card and the command structure; help within competence and keep yourself safe.

summary: You can now distinguish business continuity, critical and major incidents, give an M/ETHANE report and triage casualties with the NHS MITT. You can also describe the roles nurses play at different levels of seniority, from first on scene to the nurse in charge of a receiving ward.

A.q: Which description matches the JESIP definition of a major incident?
options: Serious consequences needing special arrangements by responders
Any event in which a patient dies unexpectedly while in a hospital
Any day when the emergency department is over capacity
Any incident that is reported to the HSE under RIDDOR
A.why: JESIP and the Cabinet Office define a major incident as an event or situation with a range of serious consequences that requires special arrangements to be implemented by one or more emergency responder agencies.

whyNot.1: An unexpected death is a serious incident, but it is not by itself a major incident.
whyNot.2: Overcrowding may be a business continuity or critical incident rather than a major incident.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers workplace injuries and is unrelated to the major incident definition.

A.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool, what is the first thing to check for in each casualty?
A.why: MITT starts with catastrophic bleeding: if present, control it with pressure, a tourniquet or haemostatic packing and categorise as P1 (NHS England, 2023).

whyNot.0: Walking is the second step, after catastrophic bleeding.
whyNot.1: Breathing is assessed after bleeding and walking.
whyNot.3: Respiratory rate is a later step in the algorithm.

A.q: A casualty at a train derailment has no catastrophic bleeding and walks over to the nurse holding his arm. What is his MITT category?
A.why: After catastrophic bleeding is excluded, any casualty who is walking is categorised P3 (NHS England MITT). He should be reassessed early, as walking casualties may be compensating for hidden injuries.

whyNot.0: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or failing later physiological checks; he is walking.
whyNot.1: P2 is reached at the end of the algorithm for non-walking casualties with normal parameters.
whyNot.3: Dead is for casualties not breathing after the airway is opened.

B.q: In an M/ETHANE report, what does the letter 'A' stand for?
B.why: M/ETHANE: Major incident declared, Exact location, Type of incident, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services (JESIP).

whyNot.0: Services present and required are covered by the final E, not A.
whyNot.2: Airway is part of casualty triage, not the M/ETHANE scene report.
whyNot.3: Agencies are covered under emergency services, the final E.

B.q: An adult casualty is not walking. When the nurse opens his airway, he does not breathe. What is his MITT category?
B.why: In MITT, a casualty who is not breathing after the airway is opened is categorised Dead. (For children under 12 after submersion, immersion or smoke inhalation, consider 5 rescue breaths if resources allow.)

whyNot.0: P1 applies to breathing casualties who fail later checks, or catastrophic bleeding.
whyNot.1: P2 is for breathing casualties with normal later parameters.

B.q: An off-duty nurse driving home comes across a multi-vehicle collision with several casualties. What should she do first?
options: Start triaging casualties at the nearest vehicle
Check the scene is safe, then call 999
Phone her ward to ask if she should attend
Move all casualties away from the vehicles
B.why: Code 15.1–15.3: offer help within competence, taking account of your own safety. Scene safety comes first, then an early, clear (M/ETHANE-style) alert to emergency services so the right response is sent.

whyNot.0: Approaching before checking safety risks her becoming a casualty too.
whyNot.2: Her ward cannot coordinate a roadside response; emergency services must be called.
whyNot.3: Moving casualties without assessment may worsen injuries and may be unsafe.

C.q: A casualty has no catastrophic bleeding, cannot walk, is breathing, answers when spoken to, is an adult, has a breathing rate of 20 and a heart rate of 108. What is his MITT category?
options: P1, as his heart rate is 100 or more
P2, as his breathing rate is normal
P3, as he responds to voice
P2, as he has no catastrophic bleeding
C.why: Working through MITT: not walking, breathing, responds to voice, over 2, breathing rate 12–23 (yes), then heart rate 100 or more: yes, so P1 (NHS England, 2023).

whyNot.1: A normal breathing rate leads to the heart rate check; a rate of 100 or more makes him P1.
whyNot.2: P3 is for walking casualties; responding to voice is a separate step.
whyNot.3: Lack of catastrophic bleeding only moves the assessment to the next step.

C.q: A major incident is declared at the local hospital. Staff Nurse Ama is in charge of a medical ward. What is her most appropriate role?
options: Send two nurses to the emergency department to help
Close the ward to new admissions until the incident ends
Wait for the incident to end before changing anything
Follow her action card, e.g. find patients fit to leave
C.why: In a hospital major incident, staff follow role-specific action cards and the command structure. Ward nurses in charge typically help create capacity, for example by identifying patients who can safely be discharged or moved, and release staff when the incident team requests them (P6.12).

whyNot.0: Self-directed redeployment can leave her ward unsafe and disrupt command and control.
whyNot.1: Closing the ward works against creating capacity for casualties.
whyNot.2: Every area has a role in the response; waiting is not appropriate.

C.q: At a fire, a nurse triages a child who looks about 18 months old. The child is not walking, is breathing and cries when spoken to. What is the MITT category?
options: P2, because the child responds to voice
P3, because the child is crying loudly
P2, because there is no catastrophic bleeding
P1, because the child appears under 2
C.why: MITT asks 'aged over 2 years?' after voice. A non-walking child judged under 2 is categorised P1, which increases P1 numbers, so early reassessment is important (NHS England MITT).

whyNot.0: Responding to voice moves to the age question, where under 2 means P1.
whyNot.1: Crying does not make a non-walking child P3; walking defines P3.
whyNot.2: No catastrophic bleeding only moves the assessment on to the next step.

reteach.title: A sieve with seven holes
reteach.question: How can one nurse sort fifty casualties in minutes?

blocks.h: Ask the same questions, in the same order
blocks.body: MITT works like a sieve: each question lets some casualties drop into a category. Stop catastrophic bleeding first. Anyone walking is P3. Not breathing with an open airway is Dead. Then voice, age, breathing rate and heart rate pick out the P1s; anyone left is P2. Because everyone asks the same questions, triage is fast and consistent, and it is repeated as people change.

blocks.h: The last checks for a breathing, non-walking adult

blocks.text: The Ten Second Triage (for any responder) uses 'not breathing' instead of 'Dead' and has no physiological measurements; MITT is the clinical tool.

explain.body: Business continuity: normal service disrupted below acceptable levels. Critical: localised loss of ability to deliver critical services. Major: serious consequences needing special arrangements by responder agencies.

test.q: A sudden surge in demand means a trust has to redeploy staff temporarily to keep services running. Under NHS EPRR, what is this?
test.why: A business continuity incident disrupts normal service delivery below acceptable levels and needs special arrangements, such as temporary redeployment, until services return to normal (NHS England EPRR).

whyNot.1: A major incident involves serious consequences needing special arrangements by responder agencies.
whyNot.2: A critical incident involves losing the ability to deliver critical services.
whyNot.3: Notifiable safety incidents relate to the duty of candour, not EPRR.

explain.body: Major incident declared or on standby, Exact location, Type of incident, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services present and required.

test.q: In M/ETHANE, which element covers the risk of fire spreading from a damaged vehicle?
test.why: H stands for Hazards, present and potential, such as fire, fuel or unstable structures (JESIP M/ETHANE).

whyNot.0: Type describes what has happened, such as a road traffic collision.
whyNot.2: Access covers routes in and out for emergency vehicles.
whyNot.3: Exact location pinpoints where the incident is.

explain.body: Catastrophic bleeding (P1), walking (P3), breathing (no: Dead), responds to voice (no: P1, recovery position), aged over 2 (no: P1), breathing rate 12–23 (no: P1), heart rate 100 or more (yes: P1; no: P2).

test.q: A casualty is breathing but does not respond when spoken to. What does MITT advise?
test.why: In MITT, a breathing casualty who does not respond to voice is placed in the recovery position and categorised P1 (NHS England).

whyNot.1: Not responding to voice is a P1 finding, and the airway needs protecting.
whyNot.3: Dead applies to casualties not breathing after the airway is opened.

explain.body: Triage is dynamic. Reassess casualties in each area, and beware of P3s: being able to walk does not exclude serious injuries that the person is compensating for.

test.q: Why should walking (P3) casualties be reassessed early?
options: They are likely to leave before being seen
They may be compensating for serious injuries
Their category must change to P2 after an hour
They need checking for catastrophic bleeding
test.why: Walking casualties may have underlying injuries they are compensating for, so early reassessment is needed (NHS England MITT guidance).

whyNot.0: Leaving is possible, but the clinical reason is hidden injury.
whyNot.2: There is no automatic time-based change in category.
whyNot.3: Catastrophic bleeding is checked first, before walking, so it has already been assessed.
